The `capture` module reports `degraded` on a role it cannot honour, which is why the example leaves the role off the Windows hosts. The public addresses use the same last octet as the internal ones. The workstations and the Kali go out through VyOS source NAT (`172.31.(20+team).2`), so they have no public address of their own [PKT §2]. Hosts with the `decoys` role never decoy on a scored port and never on a public address (the `decoys` module).

**Reference module enablement** (`manifest/2027/modules/`, builder check). The reference manifest ships one `<name>.yml` per module. The core-default modules are enabled for every host whose OS and roles satisfy their manifest (`audit`, `net`, `logs` on Linux, `winevt` on Windows, `ad` on the `domain_controller` host, `capture` on `capture` hosts, `vantage` on the Kali, and the controller modules `checks`, `scorer`, `creds` and the rest). The opt-in modules the game-day order uses are switched on where it uses them: `inventory` on every host (the baseline step), `backup` on the servers (`rocky-ecom`, `ubuntu-email`, `debian-splunk`, `ad`, `mssql`: as-found and golden backups), `decoys` and `honeytokens` on the hosts that carry the `decoys` role, `teamfeed` and `notify` on the controller. `content_guard` (per service), `vuln`, `wazuh`, `splunk` and `suricata` stay off until a team turns them on. Every block ships with `act_enabled: false`: the reference manifest starts in observe mode, and the full run flips `act_enabled` per module (fleet-wide; a per-host form is not designed) (Operations).

#### Roles and links

- **Agents in the controller's segment** dial the controller directly. On the 2027 LAN that is every host but the Kali (review D44).
- **The Kali agent** dials the controller's public address through VyOS and the Palo, under one Palo rule and one static NAT.
- **Agents in a segment that cannot reach the controller** dial their segment's relay, which splices each connection through. Chained segments chain relays (review D46, D47, D111).
- **Link direction is always child to parent** (review D48). A segment that can make no outbound connection at all would need the direction flipped for that one link; not built unless an infra requires it.
- **A dead relay** cuts its segment off. Agents there keep detecting, responding and spooling locally until it is back (review D49). Restore it with the console one-liner. No backup relay unless lab testing shows relay loss is a real problem.

#### How the relay works

The relay is a dumb splicer, which keeps it simple and keeps it from being worth attacking. It is part of the core link (the `relay` role switches it on):

- It listens on one port and accepts connections only from the source addresses in its segment's manifest entry.
- For each accepted connection it opens a new outbound TCP connection to its parent and copies bytes both ways, with deadlines and a connection cap. The agent's TLS session runs end to end to the controller, so the relay never sees plaintext and holds no agent keys.
- It keeps one outbound control connection to the controller (ALPN `phylax/relay`, its own identity), used only to receive device-proxy and bootstrap requests.
- For a **device-proxy request** the relay checks the target against its manifest allowlist, opens a connection to the device, opens a fresh outbound connection to the controller (ALPN `phylax/splice`), and splices the two. The device's own TLS stays end to end. Bootstrap downloads for hosts behind a relay use the same splice.
- Each splice records only metadata: source, destination, bytes, duration.
- There is no multiplexing layer anywhere. Every logical stream is its own TCP connection.
- **Status:** built, with no end-to-end relay test yet; that test is a gate (Testing).

#### One connection, hop by hop (Kali to controller)

Each hop needs an allow rule only in the direction the connection is opened, since all of them track connection state (review D45).

| Hop | Rule | Address used |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kali host firewall, outbound | Allow TCP to the controller's public address on the agent port | Public address |
| VyOS | Routes; source NAT to `172.31.(20+T).2` on the way out | Kali becomes the VyOS external address |
| Palo, outside to inside | Static NAT: controller public address to its internal address; allow only from the VyOS external address, only on the agent port, tagged `phylax-managed` | After NAT, the Palo sees the controller's internal address |
| Controller host firewall, inbound | Allow the agent port from the LAN agents' addresses and from the Kali's translated source only | As seen after translation |

The public NAT listener is filtered to the Kali's source address only: the organizer's perimeter assessment scores extraneous services on public addresses [[2026-mw-regional-scorecard-t7#e3]], and an agent port open to everyone is one. The controller's internal address is DHCP. A static NAT needs a fixed target, so this path depends on a DHCP reservation or on a manual rule update if the lease changes [PKT §2]. The Network role enters the Palo rule by hand at T+0; the `devices` module takes over afterwards.

#### What each firewall layer is for

- **The Palo** guards the boundary between the LAN and the outside. A host implant cannot change it without device credentials. It is also the only place that sees outside-to-LAN traffic.
- **Host firewalls** are the only control on traffic inside the flat LAN, which never crosses the Palo. An implant can disable them. Tier 0 restores them and alerts (the `firewall` and `respond` modules).
- **VyOS** is the path for every service. A lockout there is catastrophic, so changes follow the soft-revert protocol (the `devices` module).

#### Rule hygiene and bring-up

- **Separate, tagged groups** (review D50). Management rules (agent links, device access) live in their own nftables table, Windows Firewall rule group and Palo tag. Restore and drift detection treat them separately from service, dependency, decoy and inject-change rules.
- **Bring-up order** (review D51):
  1. **T+0 console phase** (Enrollment): the default passwords of the interactive admin identities rotated on the consoles, plus the urgent hardening (Zerologon first); the Palo management lockdown, the Kali-to-controller rule and the static NAT entered by the Network role from the checklist Phylax renders from the manifest.
  2. First contact installs the agents.
  3. Host firewalls get the management allows first, then (A-AUTO) default-deny inbound enforced automatically behind the scorer probe and the dead-man, with default-deny outbound installed in shadow and enforced only by a click after review (`firewall`, Execution engine).
- **Controller address.** If it changes, the static NAT is updated by hand and every agent is pointed at the new address with `phylax set-controller` on its console.

### Trust model

The controller and its unlocked keys are the only fully trusted component. Agents are trusted to report on their own host only while that host is clean. Relays, the network, host binaries, DNS and clocks are not trusted at all. The Kali is a workstation outside the Palo and is treated as an untrusted vantage point. Every mechanism below exists to keep a compromise of one host from spreading through our own tooling (review D52, D53).

#### Adversary assumptions

The red team can:

- get root or SYSTEM on any server, possibly on a workstation, possibly before drop flag
- read our full source, rules and this document
- watch or tamper with traffic inside the LAN, and across segments if they own the router
- move system clocks
- kill, patch or impersonate our agent on a host they own
- replay anything they capture
- feed crafted strings (process names, file paths, HTTP paths, usernames) into anything we log
- reach every default credential in the packet, and dump every AD hash once they hold a DC (MW Discord 2026-10-26)
- reach any local process on the controller host that is not ours

#### Trust boundaries

| Component | Trusted for | Not trusted for | If compromised |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Controller host and its unlocked keys | Everything; it is the root of trust | — | Total loss: the attacker can sign plans for every host and read the vault, including the few rotated scored passwords. |
| UI session (one login) | Launching and approving actions | — | Same as controller compromise. Bound to localhost with a login, so the attacker needs the controller host and the password. |
| Release signing key (kept off the competition network) | Which binaries are ours | — | Malicious builds. Never present in the environment. |
| Agent | Reporting what it sees while its host is clean | Truth about a compromised host; anything about other hosts | The attacker can lie for that one host, flood, replay its own history, or impersonate that host. Nothing more. |
| Kali agent | Reporting what an outside client sees | Anything else; it holds scored credentials only in memory during probes | The attacker can falsify external verdicts and read credentials in memory. Cannot command other hosts. |
| Relay | Moving bytes | Reading or altering content | Can drop or delay its segment's traffic. Cannot read, forge or command. |
| Optional OSS (Wazuh manager and others) | Extra detections and evidence | Anything on the critical path | The Wazuh manager can push code to its agents; its host is a tier-0 asset (the `wazuh` module). |
| Network devices (after rotation) | Enforcing policy | Staying unchanged | Detected by config diff; reverted from snapshot. |
| Host OS, host binaries, DNS, clocks, the network | Nothing | Everything | Assumed hostile from the start. |

#### Mechanisms

**Identity with pinned keys, no certificate authority** (review D54).

- Each agent generates its own ECDSA P-256 keypair at install and enrolls with a one-time token. The controller records the public key against the host's identity. P-256 is used everywhere because Windows SChannel (PowerShell's download path on Server 2019 and Windows 10) cannot negotiate Ed25519 server certificates [CR §2].
- The agent carries the controller's public-key hash from its bootstrap bundle.
- Both sides verify each other by key hash, not by a certificate chain, and ignore certificate dates. Moving the clock cannot break authentication.
- A stolen agent key impersonates only that host.

**Signed commands, separate from the transport** (review D55).

- Every plan step, every signed config and every control message is signed with an Ed25519 plan-signing key held only in controller memory, unlocked by passphrase.
- The step signature covers a canonical encoding (RFC 8785 JSON) of the whole step except the signature itself: plan id, node, target host identity, epoch, sequence, action, phase, parameters, a digest of the secrets blob, a digest of the rollback data, the dead-man deadline, risk class and approval record, including the approver's name [CR §3.2].
- Verification is mandatory. An agent with no plan key refuses every step and control.
- Each agent persists the highest `(epoch, seq)` it has accepted, separately for steps, controls and configs, and rejects anything not strictly greater, and any step for an unexpected plan id. The epoch rises only when the controller is restored from a snapshot (Enrollment: controller recovery).
- The transport key and the plan-signing key are different.

**Bounded agent power** (review D56). The agent runs as root or SYSTEM because it has to, but it executes only typed actions from the catalog. `host.exec` needs an explicit approval and is labeled in the UI. Pre-approved host tools are an explicit, hash-pinned list (YARA-X, `nmap` and `xfreerdp` on the Kali, the Sysmon installer, package managers installing from the depot, the services' own dump tools in backup actions).

**Per-host secrets only.** A plan step carries only the secrets its host needs. The Kali gets scored credentials only for the probes it runs, held in memory, never written to disk.

**Every endpoint is authenticated** (review D57). There is no "loopback means trusted" [CR §3.1].

| Surface | Listener | Authentication |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Agent and relay streams | `agent_port`, ALPN `phylax/*` | Mutual key pinning |
| Bootstrap downloads | `agent_port`, no ALPN | Serves only the signed binary and a bootstrap config bound to a one-time token. Mints nothing. |
| Operator UI and API | `127.0.0.1:8443` only | Login (argon2id), HttpOnly SameSite=Strict cookie, CSRF token on every state change. The CLI uses an API token created in the UI. |
| Token minting, plans, responses, approvals | UI listener only | Session plus CSRF, plus approval records for risky nodes |

**Agent data is evidence, never instructions** (review D58).

- Events are sequenced and hash-chained. The controller acknowledges what it stores. A root attacker can forge future events but cannot rewrite acknowledged ones, and gaps are visible.
- Every message is validated against its schema, with per-agent size and rate limits. Every event is validated against its declared kind and schema version.
- Nothing an agent sends is ever executed, or used to build a command or a query.

**The web UI treats every agent-supplied string as hostile** (UI shell).

**Time is for display only.** Ordering comes from per-host sequence numbers. Each heartbeat carries the host clock, and timelines apply the measured offset.

**The controller host gets the hardest hardening** (review D60). Inbound: only the agent port, from declared sources (LAN agents and the Kali's translated source). The UI is on localhost. SSH disabled. Secrets in memory only, encrypted at rest. Its own agent reports to it like any other host. Other local users and processes get nothing from the UI without the password.

**Obscurity (D-8; review D61).** The agent's install path, binary name, service name and unit name are randomised per event from a secret in the vault (built: `cmd/phylax/agent.go`, `--secret`). Sysmon's driver and service are renamed. The controller's own detections exclude the agent by its randomised path and hash, not by name. Release binaries are never mutated per host, so the signature always verifies. This raises the cost for scripted kill lists [OA §5.6, WT §9.8]. It is not a boundary.

#### Where trust is weakest

- **First contact.** A host that is already backdoored at drop flag can tamper with the agent install. Its first hunt results and its ledger sweep matter more than its heartbeats.
- **Windows.** Go calls through `ntdll` and `kernel32`, so a userland hook there affects our agent. On Linux, Go skips libc and is immune to `LD_PRELOAD`, but not to kernel rootkits.
- **The Kali.** Its verdicts are good evidence about the public path and poor evidence about anything else.
- **The controller.** The single root of trust, accepted deliberately in exchange for simplicity. A breach exposes every rotated scored password in the vault; that is one reason scored rotation is selective (review A7.Q6, A7.Q8).

### Agent runtime

The agent is the agent mode of the single static binary, running as a supervised service. It hosts agent modules, executes plan steps and holds a crash-safe spool while the link is down. Roles and the manifest switch modules on. It builds and runs on Windows as on Linux; CI cross-builds linux/amd64 and windows/amd64 with `CGO_ENABLED=0` [CR §6] (review D62).

#### Process model

- **Main process,** root or SYSTEM: everything except decoys. Modules run as supervised goroutines with panic recovery and exponential restart backoff (1 s to 60 s, reset after a 30 s stable run), and each crash emits `agent.module_crash` (built; review D63). Shared state is behind locks or channels; `go test -race` is a CI gate, because a concurrent map write is a fatal error no recover can catch [CR §3.5].
- **Decoy process,** unprivileged (a dedicated user on Linux, a low-privilege service account on Windows): every decoy listener and the fake shell. A second process, kept because decoys are the agent code most exposed to attackers. Status: the split is not done yet (docs/agent.md); the `decoys` module section carries it.
- **Config comes only from the controller** as signed `config` messages delivered at `welcome` and on change (review D65). The bootstrap file carries the controller pin and the host identity; module blocks, rules and ledger references arrive signed. An agent without config reports itself unconfigured and runs no module except `health` [CR §3.4]. The agent persists the last good config and runs it on restart without a controller.

#### Footprint

| Measure | Target | Enforced by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Binary size | 40 MB or less, 15 MB or less compressed | CI fails the build above it (`make size`; review D66). No agent-only build tag. |
| Memory | 80 MB RSS or less steady for the agent without the `capture` module, excluding kernel-held memory (reported separately in the heartbeat). On a host with the `capture` role the capture module's ring and freeze hold are Go heap (256 MiB each by default, `ring_mb` and `hold_mb`) and count on top: the hard cap is 80 MB plus the capture module's configured ring and hold, and the heartbeat reports the capture module's held bytes separately from the base figure | `debug.SetMemoryLimit` plus systemd `MemoryMax` or a Windows Job Object as the hard cap, computed from the 80 MB base plus the capture module's configured held bytes; per-module self-reported held bytes (review D67) |
| CPU | 3% average; a 5 s burst of one core at most | systemd `CPUQuota` or the Job Object; per-module self-reported usage; sweeps run at low priority; capture drops packets before slowing the host |
| Disk | Spool 200 MB cap; frozen capture evidence (pcap slices) under the `capture` module's `disk_budget_mb` (default 512 MB) | Oldest low-priority data shed first; alerts and evidence never shed (review D68) |

Kernel-held memory is reported in the heartbeat (audit backlog, inotify watches, the kernel's TPACKET_V3 mapping) [OA §5.7] but not accounted per module. The capture module's own packet ring is not kernel memory: it is a copy-in circular buffer in the agent's heap, so it counts against the cap and is sized by configuration, not hidden from it. If a lab run shows the heap ring too costly on a small host, moving it to a file is a change inside the module (the ring API does not expose where the bytes live); the design follows the code until then.

#### What "Go-native" means

- **Allowed by default:** calling the OS's own interfaces from Go: syscalls, netlink, `/proc` and `/sys`, D-Bus for systemd, Win32 APIs, COM and WMI, the event log API, LDAP and database drivers (review D86).
- **Escape hatch:** `host.exec` (Execution engine).
- **Complexity:** COM and WMI from Go (Windows Firewall, Task Scheduler, WMI subscriptions, Defender settings) is fiddly code and the largest chunk of Windows work. If one COM interface fights back, that one action uses `host.exec` and gets a complexity-register line.

#### Capabilities and the heartbeat

- **`hello` capabilities block** (review D87): kernel features, which sensors each module chose, and every registered module's manifest. This is the one capability probe; the Platform page shows it.
- **Heartbeat** every 5 s (review D99): sequence, host clock, spool depth and congestion state, safe mode, shed count, the config status (reserved module name `config`), and each module's `Health` block. Module-specific health such as audit status, fanotify overflow counts, the Sysmon service and config hash, and the hash of our own loaded audit rules comes from the owning module's `Health.Detail` and `Gaps`. Silence means the agent is down; present-but-degraded means a sensor was tampered with or overloaded.

#### Self-protection and tamper detection

No open Linux agent prevents a root user from stopping it. The goal is to raise the cost for scripted kill lists, detect fast and recover automatically [OA §5.6]:

1. **Heartbeat with sensor health** (above).
2. **Service hardening** (review D100): `Restart=always`, `RestartSec=1`, `StartLimitIntervalSec=0`, `Type=notify` with `WatchdogSec` and `sd_notify`, `OOMScoreAdjust=-900`, `MemoryMax`, `CPUQuota`, `NoNewPrivileges`, `UMask=0077` (built). Windows: automatic LocalSystem service, recovery actions restart forever (built), a protected service DACL and a Job Object cap (to build). The watchdog is `sd_notify` only today; finishing the Windows half is a core task. **The DACL must not lock the operator out:** it denies stop, pause and delete to interactive, service and batch logons and to the `BA` group, but keeps `WRITE_DAC` for `BA`, so a console administrator can `sc sdset` it back (the break-glass path); the hardening and `winevt` content already alert on `sc sdset`. The Windows halves (watchdog, Job Object, service DACL) are built and vetted in CI (the agent cross-builds for windows/amd64) but exercised for real only in the lab (W12 Task 19).
3. **Kernel-side watches on our own files** (review D101; this item and item 5 are `audit`, `winevt` and `hunt` content, built with W3 and W5, not by the enrollment work): binary, unit, config, audit rule files, through the `audit` module's file watches on Linux and `winevt` on Windows. The kernel records edits even if the agent was just killed, and the restarted agent ships them. A tier-1 alert fires if the agent binary hash changes (review D104).
4. **Opt-in immutability** (review D102): `chattr +i` on the agent binary and unit, and audit `-e 2` as an explicit late plan step with a reboot as rollback. Neither is automatic; the agent's replace-binary action clears and re-sets the bit. Already a plan step (`actions/linux_attr.go`), no new code.
5. **Cross-source tripwires** are hunt content (the `hunt` module).
6. **Assume the host key is stolen:** the controller alerts when one key is used from two places at once. The alert is the alert-class core event `enroll.key_reuse` with the detail "second live session from <addr>".
7. **Randomised names and paths** (D-8).

#### Windows Defender

An unsigned binary that captures packets, runs fake services and keeps a decoy credential session in LSASS can look like malware (review D105).

- Test the agent against current Defender definitions in the lab before every release.
- If it is flagged, hardening keeps exactly one Defender exclusion (the agent's randomised install directory) and alerts on any other exclusion.
- **Complexity:** an exclusion is a hole, even a narrow one. The only alternative is code signing, which is not practical.

#### Lifecycle

| Stage | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| Install | First contact copies the binary and a bootstrap config to a randomised path, installs a systemd unit or Windows service with automatic restart, then enrolls (review D106, `internal/svcinstall`). |
| Steady state | Supervised by systemd or the service manager. Config and rules hot-reload from signed config messages. |
| Killed or disabled | The controller sees the heartbeat stop and raises an alert (review D534). If the host is unreachable by other means, restore from the console one-liner. |
| Binary replacement | One action, `agent.replace_binary`: verify the signed binary, swap, restart, roll back if no heartbeat returns within 30 s. |
| Uninstall | One action, for cleanup after the competition (review D107). |

**The `agent.*` actions** (the Agent row of the action table): `agent.replace_binary` (above); `agent.set_controller` (the signed form of `phylax set-controller`); `agent.config{memory_limit_mb}` writes `options.json` and applies it live; `agent.rename{secret}` reinstalls the service under the names `svcinstall.DeriveNames(secret)` through the swap helper that `agent.replace_binary` uses; `agent.safe_mode{on: true}` turns safe mode on only. Turning it off stays a signed `control: safe_mode` from the UI, because the executor refuses every action while safe mode is on.

### Wire protocol and spool

Each agent holds one long-lived TLS 1.3 connection to the controller, with both sides pinning keys. Over it run length-prefixed, compressed JSON messages in strict priority order. Anything that is not agent messaging gets its own connection, told apart by ALPN. The full specification is `docs/protocol.md`.

#### TLS and pinning

- TLS 1.3 only for every agent, relay and splice connection. Bootstrap downloads also accept TLS 1.2, because Windows 10, Server 2016 and Server 2019 cannot do TLS 1.3 and the console one-liner uses the host's own stack (review D108).
- Self-signed ECDSA P-256 certificates. Verification is replaced by a check of the peer's public-key hash against the pinned value, with dates ignored.
- The controller pins each agent's key at enrollment. Agents and relays pin the controller's key from their bootstrap config.
- The TLS handshake runs in a per-connection goroutine with a pending-handshake cap and a short deadline, never in the accept loop [CR §3.3] (review D109). Go's `tls.NewListener` defers the handshake: call `HandshakeContext` before reading the negotiated ALPN (repo `AGENTS.md`).
- One listener on the controller, `agent_port`, serves every connection type. The ALPN value picks the handler (review D110, D111, D113):

| ALPN | Opened by | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `phylax/agent` | Agent (direct or spliced), including the Kali | All agent messaging |
| `phylax/relay` | Relay | The relay's control connection |
| `phylax/splice` | Relay | One device-proxy or bootstrap stream |
| None, or `http/1.1` | A host being bootstrapped from the console | Download of the agent binary and a bootstrap config bound to a one-time token. Serves only these downloads. |

The operator UI is not on this listener. Four connection types on one port is still one listener and one firewall rule, and each handler is small.

#### Framing

- Each message is a 4-byte length, a type byte (bit `0x40` flags compression) and a JSON body. Batches of events are compressed with zstd (pure Go) with a hard decoder memory cap and a size check before decompression [CR §3.6] (review D114).
- **JSON over protobuf, deliberately:** readable under pressure, no code generation.
- Maximum message size: 4 MB. Anything larger (pcap slices, files, binaries, depot blobs, alert evidence) moves as content-addressed 256 KB chunks, resumable, with `chunk_have` for resume (review D115). Alert evidence is announced by the core `evidence.blob` event (Event kinds) and capped at 8 MiB per item and 64 MiB per alert.
- Every connection has read and write deadlines and TCP keepalive. Send queues are bounded per priority. Handlers run off the receive loop so a slow handler cannot stall acknowledgments or `control` messages (review D116).

#### Messages

| Direction | Message | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Agent → controller | `hello` | Host id, agent version and protocol minor, roles, capabilities block with module manifests, last sequence, the highest `(epoch, version)` mark the agent has accepted (`epoch`; the restored controller needs it, Controller recovery), the sha256 of the agent's own running binary (`binary_sha256`; the controller compares it with the hash of the binary it served, Enrollment), dead-man entries of plan nodes, token if not yet enrolled |
| Controller → agent | `welcome` | Confirms enrollment; the first signed `config` follows |
| Agent → controller | `heartbeat` | Every 5 s: sequence, host clock, spool depth and congestion state, safe mode, shed count, per-module health, config status, and the round trip of the last heartbeat the controller echoed (`rtt_us`; the controller's `ack` carries the heartbeat `id` it answers) |
| Agent → controller | `events` | Batch of events, each with its sequence number |
| Agent → controller | `step_result` | Per-phase outcome with before and after state, signed result kept for resend |
| Both | `chunk`, `chunk_have` | Content-addressed transfers: evidence, pcap slices and collected files up; step payloads, depot blobs, ledger files and the agent binary down |
| Controller → agent | `ack` | Highest contiguous sequence stored (after the store commit) |
| Controller → agent | `step` | A signed plan step |
| Controller → agent | `config` | Signed `AgentConfig`: module blocks, rules, ledger references |
| Controller → agent | `fetch` | Request for a pcap slice, a file, a depot blob or raw telemetry |
| Controller → agent | `control` | Signed; the types are listed below: `safe_mode`, `freeze_capture`, `deadman_confirm`, `step_status`, `fact` |
| Relay ↔ controller | `relay_request` | Device-proxy and bootstrap splice requests on the relay control connection |

**Control types.** Every `control` message is signed with the plan key, host-bound and replay-protected like a step. Adding a type raises the protocol minor version, and an agent that does not know a type answers `agent.control_refused` and carries on. Adding a fact subtype does not: `fact` is the extension point.

| Type | Fields | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `safe_mode` | `on` | Suspends tier-0 responses and plan applies except the read-only actions and observe mode's allowlist; checks and rollbacks still run (Execution engine: Safe mode). Host-bound like every control; the UI request takes an optional host set and `safe_mode_hosts` in the overrides is the persistent form (Configuration) |
| `freeze_capture` | `rule`, `alert_time`, `addrs` | Freezes the packet ring for a controller-scope rule that collects `freeze_ring` (`capture`) |
| `deadman_confirm` | `node` | Disarms the dead-man for a node after the fresh-connection check |
| `step_status` | `plan`, `node`, `state` | Tells the agent a node was cancelled or superseded |
| `fact` | `id`, `fact`, `ts`, `ttl`, `data` | The one controller-to-agent mechanism for cross-host facts (builder check). The controller (a module through `Host.Control`, or the core) sends a typed fact; the agent supervisor delivers it to the on-host bus as an event of kind `controller.fact` (never spooled, so there is no echo) with the same fields. Subtypes are in the next table. An agent treats a fact it has not received, or whose `ttl` has passed, as **unknown**, and a consumer must treat unknown as "do not act" (respond's circuit breaker is the example). A later fact with the same `id` replaces the earlier one. An agent that does not know a subtype stores it and delivers it; only the subtypes marked "supervisor" below also have an effect in the supervisor |

**Fact subtypes.** A subtype is added here, never invented by a module, and has one sender and a typed `data`.

| `fact` | Sender | `data` | Consumers on the agent | Supervisor effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `work_window` | `teamfeed` | `window`, `tag`, `user`, `until`, `for`, `end` | `respond` (a window suppresses nothing; it is shown in the host record) | **Supervisor:** opens, extends or ends a tagged work window. While a window is open the emit path stamps its `tag` (the envelope `Tag` field) only on change-class kinds (`file_change`, configuration and account-change events) attributed to the claimed session or `user`; process, network, authentication and honeytoken events never get it, and the scored-service rules ignore tags (Execution engine: Tagging and adoption). The window is persisted and ends on its own after `for` (a duration counted by the agent's monotonic clock from receipt, so moving the system clock changes nothing) even with the link down; `until` is the controller's wall-clock view for display and `end` closes it early |
| `round_clock` | `scorer` | `epoch`, `delay`, `jitter`, `last_burst_end`, `window_start`, `window_end`, `min_window`, `confidence`, `provisional` | `checks` runner, `vantage` | **Supervisor:** stores the estimate for agents that hold the `check_runner` or `scanner` role. The scorer's round-clock estimate (`scorer.clock`) is sent whenever it changes; the agent extrapolates between refreshes, so a runner can hold a probe for the quiet window without asking. An agent that never receives one reports the `checks` gap `no round clock` and falls back to jittered intervals |
| `gpo_finding` | `ad` (controller side, from its `ad.gpo_finding`) | `gpo_guid`, `name`, `change`, `affects`, `enforced`, `host`, `baseline_hash`, `current_hash` | `respond` on the DC (and on members the response touches) | none; the GPO recipe reads it from the bus |
| `scorer_probe_result` | `checks` (the controller side, from the in-LAN `check_runner`'s `scorer_ok`) | `service`, `host`, `ok` (the `scorer_ok` verdict), `round`, `ts`, `source` (`lan` or `external`) | `respond` (its circuit breaker), `vantage` | none |
| `creds_txn` | `creds` | `txn`, `account`, `credlist`, `open` | `checks` runner (pauses its checks for that account while `open` is true; the fact carries a `ttl` so a lost close cannot pause it forever) | none |

**The agent `fetch` handler is a no-op today** (`internal/agent/handlers.go:41`; Known bugs). Depot pulls, ledger delivery, package installs from the depot and pcap slices all depend on it, so implementing it is a core task (review D117-D119): the agent answers `fetch` by streaming the requested object as chunks at bulk priority, bounded by the per-agent fetch cap, and the controller pushes depot blobs the same way in reverse.

#### Priority

The sender drains its queues in strict order, and every message is sent at its real priority (review D120):

1. Heartbeats, alerts, acknowledgments and dead-man confirmations
2. Plan steps and step results
3. Evidence attached to alerts
4. Transactions and flows
5. Other telemetry
6. Bulk transfers (pcap slices, files, binaries, depot blobs), shaped by a token bucket

#### Reliability

- **Spool and acknowledge** (review D121). Every event has a per-host sequence number. The agent resends from the last acknowledged sequence after every reconnect, and the controller discards duplicates.
- **Reconnect** with jittered backoff from 1 s to 30 s, round-robin over the bootstrap's controller list (review D122).
- **Per-agent limits** on message rate, bytes per minute and concurrent fetches (review D123). SQLite writes are batched in transactions.
- **Congestion states** reported to the controller: warning at 90% of the spool cap, full, flood, recovered at 70% [OA §5.8] (review D124).
- **Reorder buffer with gap records** (review D125): the controller's per-agent reorder buffer understands spool gap records (a gap covers `from..to`, so plain contiguous-sequence tracking would stall), and acks only after the store commit. `welcome` and `ack` carry no epoch or hash; the epoch travels in the signed config and steps (docs/protocol.md §6, §9).

#### Signed agent config

The signed config is the typed `AgentConfig` (`internal/plan/agentconfig.go`, docs/protocol.md §8a; review D126), generated per host by the controller from the manifest and rules, signed with the plan key, host-bound and replay-protected by a durable `(epoch, version)` mark on the agent. Versions move only when a host's content changes. It carries `roles` and `modules` (one block per agent module, nil means off). **Sealed secrets** (builder check): a secret an agent module needs on the host is carried in the signed config sealed to the host's enrolled key (the mechanism `capture` uses for its seal key), is opened in memory by the module and never written to disk or into an event; a new `(epoch, version)` is signed whenever a sealed value changes. The agent persists the last good config and runs it on restart without a controller; modules start, stop and reconfigure through the factory registry.

#### The spool

The spool is segment files, not one file [CR §3.10, OA §5.8] (review D129-D134, built in `internal/spool`):

- Append-only segments of 4 to 16 MB holding length-prefixed, CRC-checked frames. `fsync` on a bounded interval and immediately for alert-class events. A small index file holds the chain head and last-acknowledged sequence.
- **Startup repair:** scan the last segment and truncate to the last valid frame, so a torn write never bricks the agent.
- **Acknowledgment-driven deletion** of whole segments below the controller's cumulative ack, oldest first and only when space is needed, so a restored controller can ask for acknowledged data again. The chain head is persisted before any deletion.
- **Shedding is admission control, not segment deletion.** The controller store accepts each agent's chain only in contiguous sequence order, so the spool is one sequence-ordered log and transport reads it in order; priority acts at admission. Each class may fill unacknowledged space only up to its limit (critical 97%, high 90%, normal 75%, bulk 50% of the cap). An event over its class limit is not stored: it consumes its sequence number, and one **gap record** (`kind: spool.gap`, fields `from`, `to`, `count`, `class` ∈ {critical, high, normal, bulk, mixed, unknown}; `seq = to+1`; `PrevHash` bridges to the last stored event) announces the dropped run before the next stored event. History is never rewritten, and bulk can never crowd out alerts. A crash that loses a mid-log tail is reconciled at restart with a `class: unknown` gap up to the recorded head, so no sequence number is reused. Gap records are hash-chained, not separately signed. Shed order within a class: raw log lines, connection churn, flows on unscored ports.
- **Bounded RAM:** a small write buffer and an in-memory index only.
- Collection is decoupled from transport: modules write through a bounded queue, and a down link never blocks sensors or local response.
- Crash tests (kill -9 at random points, disk full, clock jumps) are a gate (Testing).

#### Volume and envelope

- **Shipped continuously:** alerts, heartbeats, process starts, connection changes, file changes on watched paths, selected log lines, flows, protocol transactions on scored ports, denied-egress attempts, decoy sightings, ledger verdicts (review D127).
- **Kept on the host until fetched:** the packet ring, raw sampler output, full log files.
- **Design envelope** (review D128): outages of up to 60 s on any link; event-to-controller latency of 10 s or less while the link is up. These size buffers and timeouts; they are targets, not competition time goals.

### Enrollment, bootstrap and recovery

The controller gets its binaries from a signed release. Before any agent exists, the team rotates the default passwords of the interactive admin identities from the consoles and does the urgent hardening (the T+0 console phase). Then the controller installs agents over SSH on Linux, over WinRM on Windows servers, and by a typed console one-liner as break-glass. Each install enrolls with a one-time token. A new reservation resets everything, so bulk re-enrollment is a first-class path. The controller itself can be restored from an encrypted snapshot kept on another host.

#### Getting binaries into the environment

1. **CI builds and signs** a release: static binaries for linux/amd64 and windows/amd64, rules and other content, YARA rules, ledger indexes, the cache index, and the pinned hash of the tested Sysmon release. Signed with an Ed25519 key that never enters the competition environment, in the sshsig signature format (the format `ssh-keygen -Y sign` produces), so anyone can verify a release with `ssh-keygen -Y verify` and no phylax binary (review D135; builder check). There is one release key. `internal/signing` implements sshsig sign and verify for release artifacts and the signed index; plan and config signing keeps its own ed25519 domain-separated scheme and is unaffected.
2. **The first binary.** The platform driver downloads `phylax` for the controller host from the GitHub release (kept small because the link is slow) and verifies it with `ssh-keygen -Y verify` (review D136). The public key to verify against is printed on the driver's checklist.
3. **`phylax init`** downloads the rest of the release, verifies it against the release key compiled into `phylax` (`internal/signing`, sshsig verify), then starts `phylax cache sync` in the background (review D19).
4. **Fallbacks,** in order: the same signed artifacts committed under `dist/`, then a build from vendored source with a Go toolchain (review D137).
5. **`phylax init` reports which channel worked** and how fast.

#### The T+0 console phase

T+0 is a console phase, not an agent phase (cross-cutting idea 5; review N7.4, A1.Q3). Team-pack admin passwords leak within seconds (a full domain dump about 10 s after drop flag at Nationals, cleartext about 20 s; decision 10), and red sprays defaults at once [[discord-2026q-rt-debrief#e1]]: 18 default-credential shells in 2026 [[how-to-win-ccdc-dealing-with-red-team]]. So before enrollment, on the consoles:

1. **Rotate every default password of the interactive admin identities, by hand.** Every host's `sysadmin`, root and local Administrator, the domain admins, the Palo `admin` and VyOS `vyos` accounts. These are the identities a person logs in as; the plan at T+0 is to rotate all the default passwords and do any immediate hardening required, like Zerologon, and nothing that could take a scored service down. Service and application accounts (OS logon accounts of services, database rows, application admin accounts) are not touched at T+0, because Phylax is not running yet and there is no lint, probe or rollback to catch a file that still embeds the old value; they rotate later by probed plan (`creds`, Rotation of unscored accounts after enrollment). No admin accounts are scored (decision 10), so admins rotate freely. Scored users are not touched. The new values are generated by Phylax from the vault once the controller is up, or from the printed T+0 sheet when it is not yet; either way the operator enters them in the vault so first contact can use them.
2. **Zerologon first on the DC** if the build is unpatched: build check, secure channel enforcement, Spooler off, SMBv1 off, before any domain rotation (the `hardening` module, `dc.zerologon_first`; review D523, D425). Red had AD through Zerologon right away [[discord-2026q-rt-debrief#e10]]; only 2 teams mitigated it in 2025 [[2025-minnesota-and-indiana-ccdc-debrief#e2]].
3. **Network devices:** Palo management lockdown (additive), the Kali-to-controller rule and static NAT, VyOS snapshot then admin rotation.

Phylax's first job afterwards is to record what was done (operators tick the T+0 steps in the host x step grid; UI shell) and, once agents arrive, to evict interactive sessions that predate the rotation (Execution engine: session eviction; sessions that own a process of a manifest service are never ended). The checklist for this phase is rendered from the manifest and printed in advance, since the UI may not be up yet.

#### First contact

First contact and enrollment are one core package, `internal/enroll` (builder check): the SSH push, the WinRM push (the `ntlm` and `winrm` protocol clients come from the shared `internal/checks/probe` library, not from the `checks` module), the console one-liner generator, the bootstrap handler on the controller's `http/1.1` ALPN, token minting and consumption, and the `phylax set-controller` command. The controller's enrollment handlers (`welcome`, `agent.enrolled`, `enroll.*` events) live there too. No module imports it; modules see its results as the core `agent.enrolled`, `agent.reenrolled` and `enroll.*` events.

| Method | When | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SSH push (preferred on Linux) | Linux hosts, reachable from the controller, with the rotated admin credentials | Built-in Go SSH client (review D138). Details below. |
| WinRM | Windows servers with WinRM enabled (Server 2019 and 2022 by default) | Built-in Go WinRM client with NTLM and message encryption, reusing the `ntlm` and `winrm` clients of `internal/checks/probe` through `internal/enroll`. Basic auth and `AllowUnencrypted` are never used (review D139, A1.Q2: build the WinRM client; no SMB-drop variant). **The push does not upload the binary:** SOAP chunks are about 4 KB, so a 40 MB binary would be roughly 9,000 round trips. The WinRM push runs the Windows one-liner through the remote shell, so the host downloads the binary from the bootstrap handler over the pinned connection; the host must reach the controller, which it must anyway. `shortcut: NTLM without message-level encryption on 5985 (signing is requested, sealing is not), upgrade when the lab finds a default Server 2019 or 2022 config refusing unencrypted SOAP over 5985`. |
| Console one-liner | Windows 11 (no WinRM by default), the Kali, Windows hosts that expose only OpenSSH, anything unreachable, and break-glass | Typed on the NETLAB console. ASCII only, short, no assumption that paste works. Downloads the binary and bootstrap config over the bootstrap connection type, checks the hash, installs (review D140). |

**The SSH push** is built from peers' working parts (COAL `coordinate-root/ssher.go@6ffc1f5`, Stanford `bootstrap/geist.sh@9485770`, UCI ember `core/ssh.go`@f2af5a1), taking only their fan-out and verify steps:

- A shell-sentinel probe confirms a usable shell; hosts with broken SSH go on a list with the next step named.
- The binary and bootstrap are uploaded base64 over stdin (no partial file on disk) to the randomised path (`shortcut: no SFTP fallback, base64 over stdin only; upgrade when a host refuses a shell command channel`, because SFTP needs a library the module list does not have); the service is installed and started.
- A banner check routes Windows OpenSSH to the console one-liner.
- A hostname check compares the host's name with the manifest entry and stops on a mismatch.
- Failures fall into a fixed set of classes (auth refused, no shell, no space, SELinux denial, timeout, hostname mismatch), and each class names its next step in the UI.
- Fan-out across hosts with a 30 s per-host timeout; success is verified by a fresh login and the agent's first heartbeat.
- Host keys are recorded at first contact and checked on later contacts. Password SSH is used only because it is what the hosts allow at T+0; hardening later follows the manifest.
- An optional single-session variant (install, rotate admin, verify by fresh login, kill old sessions) is not the default, because T+0 rotation is done by hand on the consoles (A1.Q3).

The one-liner carries two pins: the controller's public-key hash (`curl --pinnedpubkey`, or a validation callback in PowerShell, which also enables TLS 1.2 on older builds) and the download's hash. The Linux one-liner pins the SPKI hash (`--pinnedpubkey`). The Windows one-liner pins the controller certificate's SHA-1 thumbprint (`X509Certificate.GetCertHashString()` is the only hash .NET Framework 4.x exposes without extra code); `shortcut: SHA-1 thumbprint pin on Windows, upgrade when the minimum Windows build has GetCertHash(HashAlgorithmName)`. The UI generates the full command for each host [SP §A18]. Measured with a 14-character controller address and a 32-character token, the Linux line is 136 bytes and the Windows line is 294 bytes; the UI shows the exact line.

**The Invitational's console scripts (R1).** At the Invitational the typed line is the short W2 line (about 70 characters of `a-z 0-9 . : / | -`), which fetches `e.sh` or `e.ps1`, the kit, the binary and the host's bundle over plain HTTP from `phylax serve -bundles`; no pin or full hash can be typed in that time, and the pinned one-liner above stays the production path. Instead of a pin, the controller detects what a pin would have prevented: (1) the agent reports the sha256 of its own binary in `hello` (`binary_sha256`) and the controller raises an alert-class `enroll.hash_mismatch` event when it differs from the hash of the binary the controller served; (2) the controller raises `enroll.no_show` when a host that has a bundle does not connect within the enrollment window, and flags `enroll.refused` alert-class (a stolen token shows as the real host being refused); (3) bundles are served only during the enrollment window, and each `<host>.json` is removed from the served directory once that host connects, so a bundle cannot be fetched twice after use. The bundle TTL stays short. Residual risk, accepted (Risks): a trojaned binary or script that lies about its own hash is not caught.

**Bootstrap config contents** (review D141): the controller addresses and port, the controller key pin, the host's manifest identity, the randomised install parameters, the plan-signing public key, a one-time enrollment token that expires after 10 minutes, and the initial roles.

#### Enrollment

1. The UI mints a token bound to a host identity. Only a logged-in operator can do this (review D142).
2. The agent generates its keypair and connects with `phylax/agent`, presenting the token.
3. The controller records the key, binds the token to that key and replies `welcome`. The agent persists its `enrolled` flag only after `welcome`. Until then the same key may re-present the same token, so a dropped connection never wedges enrollment [CR §3.7].
4. Token consumption is atomic. A wrong-host claim does not burn a token.
5. Host identity is the manifest name plus the enrolled key, never an IP address (review D143).

#### After enrollment

SSH, WinRM and RDP are treated like any other service. If the manifest does not declare them for a host, hardening disables them, with the console as break-glass (review D144). On 2027 hosts the manifest declares SSH on the Linux hosts, WinRM on the AD host and RDP on the MSSQL host, because they are scored. Session eviction runs for every account rotated at T+0 as soon as the host's agent is up. The controller emits the core event `agent.enrolled` when it sends `welcome` for a first enrollment (host, key hash, manifest name); the `hunt` module starts its first run on it and `creds` opens the host's T+0 record (Event kinds).

#### Re-enrollment after a reset

- A per-VM reset does not exist in 2027. A new reservation resets all hosts, so the UI offers **Re-enroll all**: it revokes every old key, issues fresh tokens and runs first contact again in dependency order, after the T+0 console phase is repeated on the new hosts (review D145).
- The controller emits `agent.reenrolled` for each host that enrolls again; `hunt` starts a targeted run and `creds` marks the host's credentials reverted from it.
- **The event chain restarts at seq 1, and the store forbids that.** A new reservation gives a fresh VM, so its spool starts at 1 while the store holds `last_seq = N` for the host. `Store.ArchiveAgent` moves the old chain to the id `<host>~<n>` (tables `events`, `gaps`, `alerts`) and the host starts a new chain under its own name. `shortcut: archived rows are not re-verified under their new id, upgrade when a chain-verify command exists`.
- Every rotated credential is marked `reverted` per (account, credlist), and the hardening plans run again from zero. Every action is idempotent.
- **Quotient re-sync.** Quotient does not know about reverts: after a revert the host has the old passwords and Quotient keeps the new ones. Each reverted scored credential is either re-applied on the host or a PCR back to the old value is generated, per credlist, and the host's scored changes are blocked until it is resolved (the `creds` module, review N7.3).
- A host reset in a variant event restores its default credentials and, for the DC, rolls back every domain change. The domain credentials are marked reverted and the AD plans re-run.
- A new key claiming to be an existing host is always an alert until an operator approves it (review D146).
- After any restore or re-enrollment the prebake hunt and the ledger sweep run automatically, and the host cannot be tagged golden until both are clean [COV X-2].

#### Changing the controller address

If the address changes, run `phylax set-controller <address:port>` on each affected host's console (review D24). The Palo NAT target for the Kali path is updated by hand. Nothing is automatic.

#### Controller recovery

**State snapshot** (review D147). Every 15 minutes, and after every enrollment, plan completion and vault change (plan completion has a hook in `internal/controller/plans.go`; the vault has no change hook yet, `shortcut: vault changes wait for the next 15-minute snapshot, upgrade when the vault gets an OnChange hook`), `phylax serve` writes an encrypted snapshot to each backup target in the manifest. It holds state, not event data (target: under 10 MB): the controller's keys, enrolled agent keys with their last acknowledged sequence and chain hash, the manifest and overrides, the vault, plans and node status, active checks, the honeytoken registry, ledger overrides and incidents without bulk evidence. It is encrypted with a key derived from the operator passphrase (`age`, scrypt mode). Built in `store/backup.go` and `vault`.

**Restore starts a new epoch** (review D148). Install `phylax` on the replacement machine, fetch the latest snapshot, unlock it and start. The restored controller raises the epoch, so agents accept steps in the higher epoch despite sequence numbers the lost controller used after the snapshot. The new epoch is `max(snapshot epoch, highest epoch any agent reports in `hello`) + 1`: the snapshot holds epoch E, so restoring twice from the same or an older snapshot would otherwise produce E+1 again and agents that accepted `(E+1, s)` from the first restored controller would reject everything from the second. Until every enrolled agent has reported, the controller signs nothing and shows "restored: waiting for N agents" (agents that never return are released by an operator click, which records the epoch used). After a restore the controller asks each agent to resend everything its spool still holds, verifies that the chain passes through the snapshot's recorded sequence and hash, and marks anything missing as a gap with the reason "controller restored". The first ack after a restore lowers the agent's ack, and a spool ignores lower acks (`Spool.Ack` returns when `upTo <= s.ack`), so an agent would never resend what a restored controller lost; the spool gets `Spool.SetAck`, used for the first ack of a session only. The resend verification is not finished; it is a core task (W12 Task 12).

**Restart safety** (review D149). After any restart the controller accepts and stores agent traffic immediately. Plan signing and secret access stay locked until the passphrase is entered. **A locked controller says so (R8):** while signing is locked after a restart, the controller emits the critical, alert-class `controller.locked` event (`notify` rings and repeats until the passphrase is entered) and every page shows a red LOCKED banner on the Overview and in the header, with what is stopped (auto plans, facts, `deadman_confirm`, safe-mode toggles, the snapshot writer). The dead-man is unchanged and fail-safe: in-flight timers fire and roll back applied changes while nobody can confirm them. One flag drives the banner, the alarm and the snapshot writer's "skipped: locked" state. Packet captures, evidence files and the cache are not in the snapshot; golden service backups are copied once to the backup targets.

### Execution engine

All change goes through plans. A plan is a DAG whose nodes are typed actions on specific hosts or devices, with dependency edges and optional approval gates. Every plan shows a dry-run diff and a scoring-safety lint result before anything runs. Lockout-risk actions roll themselves back on the agent if it cannot confirm. The engine is core (`internal/plan`, `internal/actions`, `internal/deadman`, `internal/agent/exec.go`, `internal/controller/plans.go`); modules contribute actions and plan content.

#### The action contract

An action is Go code that runs either in the agent or in the controller executor (below), with four parts: **check** (is it already done, and what would change?), **apply**, **verify** and **rollback** (review D150). Each action declares a parameter schema, a risk class (`none`, `service`, `lockout`, `destructive`), the resources it locks and the **scorer-visible properties it touches** (for the lint). The framework is built:

```go
// package actions (built)
type Action interface {
	Spec() Spec                                              // name, parameter schema, risk class, platforms, Runs (agent or controller), ReadOnly
	Locks(p Params) []string                                 // named per-host resources
	Touches(p Params) []Touch                                // scorer-visible properties, for the scoring guard
	Plan(ctx context.Context, env *Env, p Params) (Plan, error)        // read-only check and dry-run diff
	Capture(ctx context.Context, env *Env, p Params) (Rollback, error) // undo data, taken under the locks before Apply
	Apply(ctx context.Context, env *Env, p Params) (Output, error)
	Verify(ctx context.Context, env *Env, p Params) error             // post-condition
}
```

A module that owns an action family registers it from its package (`actions.Register`), and lists it in its manifest's `Actions`. Controller-side actions are marked `Runs: RunsController` in their `Spec` and run in the controller executor (next subsection); they receive an `Env` with a `Probe` callback (see the scorer-mimic probe). The executor runs steps off the receive loop (8 at once; a valid step over the cap is answered `busy`, which the controller treats as retry and not as a failure, so it never triggers `on_failure`), under the locks, inside the dead-man window from the step, and rolls back by itself on an apply or verify failure (review D69).

#### The controller executor and approval classes

**The controller executor** (builder check). Some actions have no host to run on: they act on the controller's own files, on a device through its API, or on an external tool. They use the same action contract (`Plan`, `Capture`, `Apply`, `Verify`, locks, `Touches`, the lint) and are marked `Spec.Runs = RunsController` (`RunsAgent` is the default). A plan node with such an action targets the host named in the manifest as the controller (or a device); the plan engine hands it to the controller executor (`internal/controller/exec.go`) instead of sending a `step` over the link. The executor takes locks in the same namespace (`controller:<resource>` and `device:<name>`), keeps the action's rollback data in the plan record (there is no link to lose, so no dead-man), and reports the result as an `agent.step_result` event of agent `controller` (the table row for `agent.step_result` lists both executors as emitter). Its `Env` is the agent `Env` plus `Probe`, a scoped `vault.Reader` for the secret names the action declares, a depot reader and, for device actions, the device session. The controller-local actions are `pkg.fetch_to_depot` (`depot`), `wazuh.check`, `wazuh.capture`, `splunk.hec_setup`, `suricata.analyze_pcap`, `pcr.generate`, and the device adapters (`palo.*`, `vyos.*`, `device.*`, `ftd.export`).

**Approval classes** (builder check). Every plan carries one approval class, recorded in the audit trail and covered by the signature:

| Class | Who approves | What it may contain |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `click` (default) | A logged-in operator, with the named approver | Anything the lint allows. `host.exec`, `destructive` and `lockout` nodes also need their own node approval |
| `auto_readonly` | Nobody; the controller signs it with the plan key when a module calls `Host.RunReadOnly(template, params)` | Only nodes whose action has `Spec.ReadOnly = true`, risk class `none`, an empty `Touches`, and no `host.exec` outside the pinned read-only tools. The lint rule `SS000` verifies every node and refuses the plan otherwise; the plan, the calling module and the result are audited like any other |
| `standing` | An operator, once, by creating a **standing approval** | Plans whose template, targets and actions fall inside the approval's scope, until it expires |
| `auto` (A-AUTO) | Nobody per run; the controller signs it with the plan key when a module calls `Host.RunAuto(template, params)` for a template on that module's `auto` allowlist (signed manifest content) | Templates whose every node passes the **auto conditions** below. Recorded in the audit trail with the triggering event or rule and the probe results |

```go
// package plan (controller side)
type StandingApproval struct {
	ID       string
	Module   string    // the module allowed to start plans under it
	Template string    // plan template under plans/<module>/
	Targets  string    // label expression: the most it may touch
	Actions  []string  // action allowlist; risk class `lockout`, `destructive` and `host.exec` are never allowed
	Expires  time.Time // mandatory; at most the event's end
	Approver string    // the named human who approved it
	Created  string    // the operator login
}
```

A standing approval is created in the UI with one click on a proposal, shown on the Approvals page with its expiry, revoked at any time, and recorded in the audit trail with the plans that used it. `Host.RunStanding(approvalID, template, params)` checks the expanded plan against the scope on every call; a node outside it makes the whole plan fall back to `click`. The scoring-safety lint still runs on every instance, so a standing approval cannot touch scored state the lint forbids. The users are scheduled work that writes only to its own place: `backup` (periodic dumps to the backup directory; dumps are not read-only, so they run under a standing approval) and `hunt` repeats (read-only, so `auto_readonly` suffices). **Mutations need a click, a standing approval or, for the templates on a module's `auto` allowlist, the `auto` class (A-AUTO)**; `creds` plans are always `click` (the "release armed plan" is a `gate: manual` node followed by `window: scorer_quiet`), except the `resync` re-apply after a revert, which is `auto`.

**Auto conditions (A-AUTO).** `RunAuto` starts a plan only when all hold; otherwise it creates the same plan as a click proposal and says which condition failed.

1. The module's `act_enabled` is true for the target hosts, safe mode is off and the template is on the module's `auto` allowlist.
2. The scoring-safety lint passes on the controller and again on the agent, and the auto-plan rule `SS010` (its own id; `SS000` remains the read-only rule of `RunReadOnly`) checks every node of an `auto` plan: every node must be reversible by rollback data, a dead-man or a pre-change snapshot, or be read-only. A node of risk `destructive`, any `host.exec` outside the pinned read-only tools, `proc.kill_tree`, a scored-account password set outside a `resync` transaction, `ad.account.krbtgt_reset`, a device config revert and `backup.restore` (whole-service restore) is refused in an `auto` plan. These are the click-only set. The one named exception to "nothing one-way" is `ad.recycle_enable` (B1: David accepted that the Recycle Bin cannot be disabled once enabled), which runs only behind its forest-functional-level check.
3. Every node that touches a scored service (its `Touches` hits a manifest-scored service) runs the scorer-mimic probe before and after, inside the node, with one probe per host and phase for nodes sharing a lock set, and `deadman_confirm` waits for the after-probe (Execution engine: the scorer-mimic probe). **If the probe cannot run** (link down, no `health:` block, no vault credential for the probe, an unknown `scorer_probe_result` fact), the `auto` plan is not started and becomes a click proposal.
4. A failed after-probe rolls the node back automatically (the existing rule); a failed before-probe stops the node. `on_failure` for an `auto` plan is `rollback_plan`.
5. A **circuit breaker per (module, template, host)**: two automatic rollbacks of the same template on a host within 10 minutes disable that template's `auto` class on that host, emit `plan.auto_halted` (critical) and need an operator to re-enable it. A template that fires again right after a clean apply (red reverting it) is stopped by the module's loop detection, as for tier 0.
6. The plan's `Approver` field records `auto:<module>/<template>` and the triggering event id.

#### Action families

Action names follow the code. Where the code registers a name (`internal/actions`), the name is final and this table uses it; a name marked *new* is specified here or in the owning module's section and not registered yet. One name has one owner and appears in one row. The core owns the general families that many modules' plans use. A module that owns a family specifies it in its module section (risk, locks, scorer-visible touches), registers it from its package and lists it in its manifest's `Actions`; the manifest `Actions` lists are checked against this table in CI.

| Family | Actions | Linux | Windows | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Files | `file.write`, `file.template`, `file.perms`, `file.quarantine`, `file.restore`, `file.hash`, `file.attr` (clear or set immutable), `dir.snapshot` (*new*) | Native; atomic temp-and-rename that copies mode, owner, xattrs and SELinux label; `validate` hook | Native | core (review D151) |
| Local accounts | `user.set_password`, `user.lock`, `user.create`, `user.delete`, `group.members`, `ssh.authorized_keys`, `session.terminate_predating` (*new*; ends only interactive logon types and never a session that owns a process of a manifest service, see Session eviction) | Edit `/etc/shadow` and friends under the shadow-utils lock (`lckpwdf`), atomically, preserving aging fields and labels; SHA-512 crypt; clears and restores `chattr +i` on `/etc/shadow` and `/etc/passwd` | `NetUserSetInfo`, `NetLocalGroup*`, WTS session APIs | core (review D152, N3.1, N3.3) |
| Services | `service.state`, `service.config`, `systemd.dropin`, `cockpit.disable`, `win.service.config` | systemd over D-Bus; `validate` hook on config | Service control manager APIs | core (review D154) |
| Config edits | `ini.set`, `conf.set`, `xml.set`, `agentopt.set` (agent options, e.g. Wazuh agent settings) | Native, in place, with the `validate` hook | Same | core |
| Registry | `registry.set`, `registry.delete`, `registry.snapshot` (*new*) | — | Native registry API; `registry.set` and `registry.delete` are the built names (the earlier draft said `reg.*`) | core (review D158) |
| Kernel and system | `sysctl.set`, `kernel.module_block`, `mount.remount` (*new*), `hosts.file` (*new*), `selinux.restore` (*new*) | `/proc/sys`, modprobe config; `mount.remount` changes the options of a mounted path (risk `service`, lock `mounts`, touches the mount options of the path, rollback remounts the prior options; the `hardening` noexec pack uses it) | — | core (review D157). The unused `modules.disable_loading` action is deleted. `kernel.module_block` verify is fixed (Known bugs 1). The earlier draft's `module.block` is `kernel.module_block` |
| Persistence cleanup | `cron.disable`, `at.disable`, `unit.disable` (*new*), `unit.mask` (*new*), `task.disable` (*new*), `wmi.subscription_remove` (*new*), `runkey.remove` (*new*), `ld_preload.clear` (*new*), `caps.clear` (*new*), `pkg.unhold` (*new*) | Native file edits, D-Bus | Task Scheduler and WMI through COM; registry | core (review D159). Every hunt finding ends here; disable and quarantine, never delete. |
| Processes | `proc.kill_tree` (pidfd plus start-time check; `cgroup.kill` for units), `proc.suspend`, `proc.dump` (all *new*) | Signals, cgroup freeze, `/proc/<pid>/mem` | `TerminateProcess`; `MiniDumpWriteDump` | core (review D160). Collected samples and dumps are defanged (ELF or PE magic zeroed) so a stored sample cannot execute or trip AV. |
| Logging | `audit.rules`, `audit.immutable` (*new*; owned by `audit`), `win.audit_policy.set` (built; the earlier draft's `auditpol.set`), `eventlog.size` (*new*), `sysmon.install`, `sysmon.config` (*new*), `win.defender`, `win.defender.audit` | Kernel audit over netlink | Native audit-policy API; `sysmon.install` uses `host.exec`; the Defender actions use the Defender API | core (review D161), except `audit.rules` and `audit.immutable`, which the `audit` module registers and implements against its own rule set (builder check) |

Dumps and restores are `backup.*`, not here |
| Web and application | `web.opencart_audit`, `web.rename_dir`, `web.remove_dir`, `web.roundcube_audit` (*new*) | Native | Same | core (the `hardening` packs use them) |

The dead-man rollback handlers `fw.nft.restore` and `fw.win.restore` are handler kinds the dead-man journal names, not plan actions |

The earlier draft's `ldap.modify` is dropped: no plan needs a write the `ad.account.*` and `ad.gpo_*` actions do not cover |

Scheduled dumps run under a standing approval (controller executor and approval classes); restores need a click |
